The Voyager Mission

A two-spacecraft NASA mission that began as a four-year trip to Jupiter and Saturn and became a fifty-year journey through the outer solar system and into interstellar space.

Origins

How the mission began

In the 1960s, planetary scientists noticed that the outer planets were about to line up in a way that would allow a single spacecraft to visit several of them using gravity assists — roughly once every 175 years.

NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory built two nearly identical probes designed to survive the harsh environment of the outer solar system — and, if fortune allowed, to keep going far beyond it.

Launch

The 1977 launches

Voyager 2 lifted off first on 20 August 1977 on a slower trajectory. Voyager 1 followed on 5 September 1977 on a faster path. Both launched from Cape Canaveral, Florida.

Each spacecraft carried ten science instruments (radio science, using the communications system, is sometimes counted as an eleventh), a 3.7-metre dish antenna, three radioisotope power generators producing about 470 watts at launch, and a Golden Record greeting from Earth.

Grand Tour

Four planets, one alignment

Jupiter · 1979

Both spacecraft revealed Jupiter’s turbulent atmosphere and discovered active volcanoes on its moon Io.

Saturn · 1980–1981

Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 revealed a ring system of extraordinary complexity and studied Titan’s atmosphere.

Uranus · 1986

Voyager 2 made the only close flyby of Uranus, finding a lopsided magnetic field and ten new moons.

Neptune · 1989

Voyager 2 discovered the Great Dark Spot, supersonic winds and geysers on Triton.

Voyager 1’s close flyby of Saturn’s moon Titan bent its path north, ending its Grand Tour — a deliberate trade for Titan data. Voyager 2 went on to become the only spacecraft to visit Uranus and Neptune.

Beyond the planets

From the heliosphere to interstellar space

Around the Sun, the solar wind carves out a bubble called the heliosphere. Its outer boundary is the heliopause — where the pressure of the solar wind meets the plasma of the galaxy.

Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause on 25 August 2012 at about 121 AU from the Sun; Voyager 2 followed on 5 November 2018 at about 119 AU.

The extended mission

Mission extension and long-term goals

The planetary mission ended with the Neptune flyby in 1989. On 1 January 1990 the Voyager Interstellar Mission formally began, with a new goal: to explore the outer heliosphere and cross into interstellar space. Along the way Voyager 1 passed the termination shock — where the solar wind abruptly slows — in December 2004 at about 94 AU, and Voyager 2 did so in August 2007 at about 84 AU, a first sign that the heliosphere is not a perfect sphere.

A note on power

Each probe’s power supply loses about 4 watts a year as its plutonium decays and its thermocouples age. To stay within budget, NASA switches off heaters and instruments in a sequence planned years ahead; as of 2026 Voyager 1 runs two science instruments and Voyager 2 three. Current status is shown on each spacecraft page.

In order

The mission in one line

1977 launches → Jupiter 1979 → Saturn 1980–81 → Uranus 1986 → Neptune 1989 → Pale Blue Dot 1990 → Voyager 1 in interstellar space 2012 → Voyager 2 in interstellar space 2018 → interstellar operations continue today. Explore the full timeline
